question: Why do drivers often say they never saw the motorcycle before a crash?
choice_a: Motorcycles are required to be painted black
choice_b: A motorcycle's outline is much smaller than a car's, and it's difficult to see something you are not looking for
choice_c: Motorcycles are always faster than the vehicles around them
choice_d: Drivers are legally not required to look for motorcycles
explanation: From ahead or behind, a motorcycle's outline is much smaller than a car's; it's difficult to see something you are not looking for, and most drivers are not looking for motorcycles.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.25, 'Increasing Conspicuity'

question: What mindset does the manual suggest riders adopt to stay hyper-aware?
choice_a: Assume every driver has already seen and will yield to you
choice_b: Ride as though no other traffic exists
choice_c: Pretend you're invisible, assuming other motorists can't see you
choice_d: Assume drivers are always looking specifically for motorcycles
explanation: A good strategy is to pretend you're invisible -- if you assume other motorists can't see you, you'll tend to ride in a hyper-aware mindset and notice more details in your surroundings.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.25, 'Increasing Conspicuity'

question: Even if a driver does see a motorcyclist approaching, why might they still pull out in front of the rider?
choice_a: Drivers are legally required to pull out regardless of oncoming traffic
choice_b: Motorcycles are invisible to human vision even in daylight
choice_c: It never happens once a driver has made eye contact
choice_d: Smaller vehicles appear farther away than they actually are, so drivers often think they have plenty of time
explanation: Even if a driver does see you coming, you aren't necessarily safe -- smaller vehicles appear farther away than they actually are, so it's common for drivers to pull out in front of motorcyclists thinking they have plenty of time.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.25, 'Increasing Conspicuity'

question: What colors of jackets or vests does the manual identify as the best bets for being seen?
choice_a: Bright orange, red, yellow, or green
explanation: Bright orange, red, yellow, or green jackets/vests are the best bets for being seen; any bright color is better than drab or dark colors, and reflective, bright-colored clothing is best.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.25, 'Clothing'

question: According to the manual, what fraction of the visible surface area of the rider/motorcycle unit does the rider's body make up?
explanation: Wear bright-colored clothing to increase your chances of being seen; remember, your body is half of the visible surface area of the rider/motorcycle unit.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.25, 'Clothing'

question: Where can reflective material help drivers spot a rider most?
choice_a: Only on the bottom of the motorcycle where it can't be seen
choice_b: Reflective material provides no benefit at night
choice_c: On the vest and the sides of the helmet, helping drivers coming from the side, ahead, or behind
explanation: Reflective material on a vest and on the sides of the helmet will help drivers coming from the side spot you, and can also help drivers both ahead and behind.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.25, 'Clothing'

question: According to studies cited in the manual, how does riding with the headlight on during the day affect a motorcycle's visibility?
choice_a: It has no effect during daylight hours
choice_b: It makes the motorcycle harder to see in daylight
choice_c: It is only effective at night
choice_d: A motorcycle with its light on is twice as likely to be noticed during the day
explanation: A good way to help others see your motorcycle is to have the headlight on at all times; studies show that during the day, a motorcycle with its light on is twice as likely to be noticed.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.25-26, 'Headlight'

question: When should a rider use the low beam headlight?
choice_b: Only during the day in clear weather
choice_c: Low beams should never be used on a motorcycle
explanation: Use low beam at night and in fog.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.26, 'Headlight'

question: Why should riders use their turn signals even when what they plan to do seems obvious?
choice_a: It is only a suggestion with no real safety benefit
choice_b: Signal lights make you easier to spot and reduce confusion for the traffic around you
choice_c: Signals are only required at night
choice_d: Turning on a signal has no effect on visibility
explanation: Due to a rider's added vulnerability, signals are even more important; use them anytime you plan to change lanes or turn, even when what you plan to do is obvious, since your signal lights make you easier to spot.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.26, 'Signals'

question: Why is it important to turn off your signal after completing a turn?
choice_a: It has no consequence if left on
choice_b: Signals turn off automatically on all motorcycles
choice_c: A driver may pull directly into your path thinking you plan to turn again
choice_d: It is only a courtesy with no safety implication
explanation: Once you turn, make sure your signal is off, or a driver may pull directly into your path, thinking you plan to turn again.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.26, 'Signals'

question: Why should a rider flash the brake light before slowing down in certain situations?
choice_a: Flashing the brake light increases stopping power
choice_b: It is required only when coming to a complete stop
choice_c: Brake lights should never be flashed under any circumstance
choice_d: A motorcycle's brake light is usually not as noticeable as a car's, so flashing it helps others notice you're slowing
explanation: A motorcycle's brake light is usually not as noticeable as a car's brake lights; if the situation permits, help others notice you by flashing your brake light before you slow down.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.26, 'Brake Light'

question: In addition to checking mirrors, what else should a rider do before changing lanes?
choice_a: Turn their head and look to the side for other vehicles (a head check), since motorcycles have blind spots too
choice_b: Nothing further is needed once mirrors are checked
choice_c: Only check the mirror on the side opposite the intended lane change
choice_d: Rely solely on the turn signal to clear traffic
explanation: Checking your mirrors is not enough -- motorcycles have blind spots like cars. Before changing lanes, turn your head and look to the side for other vehicles.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.27, 'Head Checks'

question: What type of mirrors do most motorcycles have, and what is their advantage?
choice_a: Flat mirrors only, which provide the widest view
choice_b: Rounded (convex) mirrors, which provide a wider view of the road behind than flat mirrors
choice_c: No mirrors are standard equipment on motorcycles
choice_d: Concave mirrors, which magnify distant objects
explanation: Most motorcycles have rounded (convex) mirrors, which provide a wider view of the road behind than flat mirrors, though they also make cars seem farther away than they actually are.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.27, 'Using Your Mirrors'

question: What should a rider do to compensate for riding at night, when it is harder to see and be seen?
choice_a: Ride faster to get home sooner
choice_b: Keep the same following distance used during the day
choice_c: Reduce speed, increase following distance, use the car ahead's headlights, use the high beam when not following or meeting a car, and be flexible about lane position
choice_d: Always use the low beam even on empty rural roads
explanation: At night, reduce speed, increase distance (open up a three-second or more following distance), use the car ahead's headlights for a better view, use the high beam whenever not following or meeting a car, and be flexible about lane position.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.27-28, 'Riding at Night'

question: What does the manual mean by "Do Not Override Your Headlight" at night?
choice_a: Never use the headlight at all
choice_b: Always use the highest-wattage bulb regardless of legality
choice_c: Ride only during daylight to avoid the issue
choice_d: Do not let your total stopping distance exceed the distance your light beam illuminates
explanation: Do not override your headlight -- do not let your total stopping distance exceed the distance your light beam illuminates; slow down so you can stop within the distance you can see.
source_note: Alabama Motorcycle Operator Manual (18th Ed., Oct. 2024), p.28, 'Riding at Night'
